cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Try It First
cards.instruction: Get someone else to test the shortcut, substitute, or questionable fix before you rely on it.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Taste this cheap coffee substitute before I fill my cup.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. If you like this, we can save the proper stuff for guests.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'm not sacrificing breakfast to save you money.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: One sip. If it's awful, I'll buy you a croissant and keep my cup empty.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 and A3 announce authority, but A5 ordinary bargain for one sip drops the approval relationship.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 proper-coffee availability causes A3 guest-saving rationale; B4 breakfast refusal causes A5 croissant compensation, after an irrelevant restriction.

relationship.evidence: B2 offers a usable alternative and B4 protects breakfast enjoyment, giving the test real personal cost.

heightening.evidence: B4 refusal reduces the requested exposure to one sip while A5 promises compensation and keeps A cup empty.

specificity.evidence: A1 cheap substitute before filling A cup establishes the exact trial-before-reliance sequence.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 empty-cup condition is earned by the test refusal; the generic A3 command interrupts natural bargaining.
